newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelan airline Viasa to be liquidated.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan airline Viasa to be liquidated.

text.p: Shareholders of the grounded Venezuelan airline Viasa agreed Thursday to liquidate the company within a year, a member of the board said.

The decision ended a month of sometimes bitter negotiations between Spain's national carrier Iberia, Venezuela's national Investment Fund (FIV), the body in charge of privatisations, and employees to save the country's flagship airline from bankruptcy.
Iberia, which took over Viasa management in 1991, held the largest stake in the loss-making airline with 45 percent.

"The shareholders proposed to instruct the company's administration to ask for the competent court's permission to move toward ... the amicable liquidation of its business within a period not exceeding 12 months," William Bracho, workers' representative on Viasa's board of directors, said.
He read the announcement to reporters at the end of an extraordinary shareholders' meeting.
Viasa suspended all its flights on Jan. 23 after workers overwhelmingly rejected an emergency rescue plan that involved job cuts and route reductions.
The airline, in which the FIV owns 40 percent and the country's largest bank, Banco Provincial, 15 percent, has debts totalling more than $150 million, according to unfinished audits.

The FIV said in a statement the decision to liquidate Viasa was inevitable "although since the start of talks (the FIV) has always been oriented toward seeking the best alternatives to save the company."
The decision to close Viasa, which employs about 2,250 people and has a fleet of 10 aircraft, was taken in spite of a preliminary accord reached on Jan. 28 between Iberia and the FIV.

It included a $30-million pledge from Iberia and $25 million from the Venezuelan government to recapitalize the company and a promise to seek an investor to operate the carrier. The plan also involved job cuts.
But, amid strident accusations of mismanagement, corporate plunder and corruption, the government had hinted in recent days it was not prepared to inject fresh capital to save Viasa.
